page: Amazon Web Services r5.24xlarge is a memory-optimized server instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture with 96 virtual CPUs mapped to 48 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor operating at 3.1 GHz. The system includes 768.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPUs, relying instead on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps.

Benchmark results indicate strong multi-core performance and memory throughput. The instance achieves a stress-ng multi-core CPU score of 80919.72 and a PassMark CPU score of 55744.75, placing it in the top tier for multi-threaded workloads. Memory bandwidth is highly efficient, reaching 4503.04 GB/sec for cached small-block reads and 220.3 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads. However, single-core performance is relatively weak, as evidenced by a stress-ng single-core score of 1383.99 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1160.0.

The high memory-to-vCPU ratio and strong database performance, highlighted by 74.62 million operations per second in Redis SET benchmarks and 21687.95 in PassMark database operations, make this instance highly cost-efficient for memory-intensive applications. Conversely, it is less suited for single-threaded tasks or intensive LLM text generation, where it registers lower performance metrics. The r5.24xlarge is best suited for large in-memory databases, high-throughput web serving, and memory-intensive data processing workloads.

It is configured with 96 vCPUs, 48 physical cores, and 768.0 GB of DDR4 memory, yielding a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. The instance lacks local storage and GPUs but delivers a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps. Performance benchmarks show strong multi-core capabilities, with a PassMark CPU score of 55744.75, and exceptional memory bandwidth, reaching 220.3 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads. It also demonstrates high efficiency in database operations, executing 74.62 million Redis SET operations per second. However, single-core performance remains a tradeoff, with a stress-ng single-core score in the bottom 25%. This instance is highly suited for memory-intensive workloads, including large-scale in-memory databases, caching layers, and high-throughput data processing.
